_about: National guidance layer shown alongside the regional monograph text. Each item carries `verified`: true when the wording was checked against the source text or an official summary; false when it comes from secondary reporting and must be checked against the full guideline by the editorial group before clinical use.

bsr2025.title: BSR guideline for the prescription and monitoring of csDMARDs
bsr2025.status: Published 2025 (Rheumatology 65(2), keaf522). Replaces the 2017 BSR/BHPR guideline. Takes precedence over the regional text where they differ.

general.text: Covers the whole life course (children, young people and adults). Biologics, JAK inhibitors and apremilast are out of scope and sit in the separate b/tsDMARD safety guideline.
Five sections: pre-treatment evaluation, drug-specific recommendations, comorbidities, blood-test monitoring, and shared care.
Blood monitoring is risk-adaptive rather than one schedule for everyone. Risk factors for csDMARD toxicity should be reassessed at least annually and the monitoring interval adjusted.
Baseline full blood count, renal profile and liver profile are strongly recommended before starting a csDMARD, to detect pre-existing cytopenia and organ impairment.

Monitoring in the first six months is less frequent than under the 2017 guidance. Secondary summaries describe a check at week 2 then monthly for the first 3 to 6 months in patients without added risk factors; confirm against Table 3 of the full text.

On a stable dose without risk factors: FBC, renal function, ALT/AST and albumin about every 3 months, with the interval extendable after an individual benefit–risk assessment (some stable low-risk patients may need only one or two tests a year).

Liver biochemical abnormalities are not an absolute contra-indication to any csDMARD, but a less hepatotoxic drug (for example sulfasalazine) is preferred and monitoring should be more cautious. Established fibrosis or cirrhosis: avoid hepatotoxic csDMARDs.
During a severe infection (needing intravenous therapy or admission) csDMARDs should be stopped temporarily until the patient has recovered.
Shared care: coordinated arrangements between rheumatology and primary care, with clear responsibilities for prescribing, monitoring and acting on results.
Voclosporin is newly included as a csDMARD (lupus nephritis).

methotrexate.text: Adults with risk factors for liver disease: calculate a FIB-4 score before starting, followed by elastography (e.g. FibroScan) if indicated. This should not delay starting methotrexate.
After influenza or COVID-19 vaccination in adults, methotrexate may be withheld for up to two weeks if disease activity and flare risk allow. In children this is at the clinician's discretion.
Agree a fixed weekly dosing day and co-prescribe folic acid.

hydroxychloroquine.text: No routine blood monitoring is required (as in 2017). Monitoring is for retinopathy.
Everyone who has taken hydroxychloroquine for the equivalent of 5 years' continuous treatment or more should have annual retinopathy monitoring (GRADE 1B, 100% agreement).
Patients at high risk of retinopathy should have annual monitoring after 1 year of use.

sulfasalazine.text: Preferred where liver biochemistry is abnormal, as a less hepatotoxic csDMARD.
Sulfasalazine, mepacrine and apremilast join hydroxychloroquine as drugs where long-term routine blood monitoring is reduced or not required once stable; confirm the exact wording in the full text.

leflunomide.text: Blood pressure and weight monitoring continue alongside blood tests; confirm the intervals in Table 3 of the full text.

azathioprine.text: TPMT activity or genotype before starting remains recommended; confirm wording in the full text.

mycophenolate-mofetil.text: Standard risk-adaptive blood schedule applies; confirm any drug-specific points in the full text.

cyclosporine.text: Renal function and blood pressure are the key monitoring parameters; confirm the intervals in Table 3 of the full text.

tacrolimus.text: Included in the 2025 guideline. No regional page exists yet.

voclosporin.text: Newly included in the 2025 guideline (lupus nephritis). No regional page exists yet.

bsr2019.title: BSR biologic DMARD safety guidelines in inflammatory arthritis
bsr2019.status: Current national guidance for biologics. An update covering JAK inhibitors, IL-17 and IL-23 inhibitors and children/young people is in progress; the published scope (Ling et al., Rheumatol Adv Pract 2025, doi 10.1093/rap/rkaf104) says publication is expected 2026/27.

general.text: Screen for tuberculosis (history, examination, chest radiograph and an interferon-gamma release assay or tuberculin test) before starting; treat latent TB before or alongside the biologic.
Screen for hepatitis B (surface antigen and core antibody), hepatitis C and, where risk factors exist, HIV before starting.

Check vaccination status before starting. Live vaccines are contra-indicated on treatment; give them at least 2 and ideally 4 weeks before starting. Inactivated vaccines (influenza, pneumococcal, COVID-19) are recommended.
Peri-operative: for elective surgery, plan the operation at the end of the dosing interval and restart once the wound has healed and there is no infection.
Biologics should be stopped during serious infection and withheld in active infection.
Patients with a previous malignancy: individual benefit–risk decision; rituximab may be preferred in some situations. Regular skin checks are advised.

The 2026/27 update will add: ANA testing before a first TNF inhibitor, prescribing choices in people at high infection, VTE or cardiovascular risk, CTD-ILD, drug-induced uveitis, psoriasis and IBD, updated peri-operative guidance (one dosing interval off; restart about 14 days after surgery) and vaccination intervals.

mhra2023.title: MHRA Drug Safety Update: JAK inhibitors, new measures to reduce risks of MACE, malignancy, VTE, serious infections and mortality
mhra2023.org: Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency
mhra2023.status: Applies to baricitinib, filgotinib, tofacitinib and upadacitinib (and abrocitinib). Based on the ORAL Surveillance trial of tofacitinib against TNF inhibitors.

general.text: Use a JAK inhibitor only if no suitable alternative is available in patients aged 65 or over, current or past long-time smokers, and those with other risk factors for cardiovascular disease or malignancy.
Use with caution in patients with risk factors for venous thromboembolism other than those above.
Consider a reduced dose in patients at risk where the product information allows (for example tofacitinib 5 mg twice daily, baricitinib 2 mg).
Periodic skin examination is recommended for all patients, particularly those at increased risk of skin cancer.
Counsel patients on the symptoms of blood clots, cardiovascular events and cancer and to seek help promptly.

greenBook.title: Immunisation against infectious disease (the Green Book)

general.text: Live vaccines are contra-indicated in significant immunosuppression (for example methotrexate above 25 mg/week, azathioprine above 3 mg/kg/day, high-dose steroids, biologics and JAK inhibitors). Shingrix (recombinant, non-live) can be used instead of the live shingles vaccine.
